questions.q: What is the main engineering difference between the performance measures from Chapter 5 and live strategy monitoring?
options: There is no real difference; live monitoring simply reruns the same report once a year
Live monitoring requires the same ideas (P&L, drawdown, risk limits) running continuously as code, so problems can be acted on immediately rather than discovered after the fact
Live monitoring never needs to track drawdown
Chapter 5's measures cannot be computed at all once a strategy goes live
questions.explain: A backtest report is computed once over a finished series. Live monitoring needs the same underlying ideas running continuously, as automated code, so that risk problems can trigger an immediate response instead of being noticed only in a later review.

questions.q: What is the defining purpose of a kill switch?
options: To optimize the strategy's parameters in real time
To automatically stop trading (and often flatten positions) the moment a pre-defined hard risk limit is breached, removing in-the-moment human hesitation
To notify a human without taking any automatic action
To permanently delete a strategy's historical records
questions.explain: A kill switch is a hard, automatic, pre-committed rule: when a defined limit is breached, it stops new orders and often flattens positions immediately, specifically to avoid the human 'wait and see' hesitation that can make a real crisis worse.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which situations should trigger an automatic kill switch versus a human alert?
options: Every anomaly, no matter how small, should trigger an automatic kill switch
Nothing should ever be automated; a human should always be the one to decide
Hard, pre-committed risk limits (max daily loss, max drawdown, max position size) belong in the kill switch; softer warning signs (unusual but non-breaching activity) belong in a human alert
Alerts and kill switches are two names for the exact same mechanism
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes genuinely hard, pre-committed limits (which should auto-stop trading) from softer anomalies that warrant notifying a human without an automatic stop, since confusing the two in either direction causes real losses in practice.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, realized live daily P&L volatility was 1.83 times the backtest's expected volatility. What should this trigger?
options: An automatic kill switch, since any deviation from backtest expectations must stop the strategy
Nothing at all, since live and backtest volatility are never expected to match
A review, since a growing gap between realized and expected behavior can be an early sign of strategy decay, even though one bad day in a short sample isn't conclusive on its own
A permanent retirement of the strategy with no further analysis
questions.explain: A large realized-vs-expected volatility ratio is a signal worth investigating, not an automatic kill-switch trigger on its own — especially given how much a single bad day can move this ratio in a short sample, echoing Lesson 25's point about sampling noise. A sustained, growing gap over time is the real signal.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend logging every order, fill, risk check, and alert in an operational log?
options: Logs are only useful for regulatory compliance and serve no other purpose
It turns an unanswerable question ("the strategy lost money last Tuesday, not sure why") into a reconstructable one, by recording exactly what happened and in what order
Logging is unnecessary if the strategy has a kill switch
Only risk-limit breaches need to be logged, not successful checks
questions.explain: A detailed operational log — including every risk check performed and its result, not just breaches — lets you reconstruct exactly what happened after the fact, turning a vague question about an unexplained loss into something that can actually be answered.
